clue.text: Legendary weapon's former quality spoken of

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: something spoken of is heard rather than seen, so the sound of the phrase gives the spelling

parts.note: EX means former and CALIBRE means quality, giving a phrase said as one word

explanation.surface: A mythical sword's old-time excellence is being talked about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spoken of' signals that EX-CALIBRE (former quality), said out loud, matches the name of King Arthur's sword.
explanation.definitionFit: King Arthur's sword in the old legends is the most famous mythical blade.

clue.text: Measure satisfied social worker

parts.note: an em is a unit of measure in printing
a need that is met is satisfied

explanation.surface: A council employee in social services seems content with their assessment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'social worker' suggests a council job; it is an ant, a social insect. Emmet is an old or dialect word for an ant.
explanation.definitionFit: Ants live in organised colonies and are classic social insects; emmet is an old name for one.

clue.text: Small business has building ground perhaps by railway

parts.note: a cottage is a small house, so a building
by can mean in, as in 'by day' for 'in the day'
ground matter, powdered fine, is dust

explanation.surface: A small firm owns premises on a plot of land next to the railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'building' and 'ground' read like property, but they give COTTAGE and DUST.
explanation.definitionFit: A cottage industry is a small-scale business, often worked from people's homes.

clue.text: Most careful to avoid risk of crossing lake

clue.text: UK bachelor standing on ceremony mainly

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'UK bachelor standing on ceremony mainly', gives B on RIT(e), but 'UK' alone cannot stand for a British person; a word of the definition looks missing.
annotationWithheld.clue: UK bachelor standing on ceremony mainly

clue.text: One got up badly wanting paper and a bread roll

parts.note: a rag is slang for a low-quality newspaper
a muffin is a flat round bread roll, the English kind

explanation.surface: Someone poorly dressed is hungry for a newspaper and a bread roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got up' means dressed: a ragamuffin is a scruffy child in ragged clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragamuffin is a person, often a child, in ragged dirty clothes, so badly dressed.

clue.text: Opening test over in South Africa

indicators.note: the clue's 'in' puts the reversed test between the two letters for South Africa
over tells us to turn the word for a test the other way round

parts.note: the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for British cars

explanation.surface: A trial is complete somewhere in South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' is the reversal signal and 'in' the container. The MOT is Britain's yearly roadworthiness test for cars.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology and surgery a stoma is a small mouth-like pore or artificial hole.

clue.text: Idiot applies for flipping badge!

indicators.note: flipping turns the word for applies over, so it reads backwards

parts.note: to apply something, like paint, is to put it on
an ID badge shows who you are, so badge gives ID

explanation.surface: An exasperated person calls someone a fool for wanting a stupid badge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' looks like a mild British swear word, but it turns PUTS into STUP. Stupid as a noun is a casual insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone 'stupid' as a noun, as in 'Look, stupid', means calling them a fool.

clue.text: I'm paid, see — no longer working

definitions.text: I'm paid, see — no longer working

parts.words: I'm paid, see — no longer working
parts.note: read as someone who gets money without having a job, because they have retired and draw a state pension

explanation.surface: Someone explains they still get money even though they have stopped work.
explanation.definitionFit: A retired person drawing a state pension is paid though no longer employed.

clue.text: From Gulf state departs leaving for the old country

parts.note: a gulf is a huge gap or chasm, an abyss

indicators.note: leaving means the letter for departs goes out of the country's name

parts.note: India is a state, meaning a nation
D is the timetable abbreviation for departs

explanation.surface: Someone leaves a Gulf nation for their former homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gulf state' suggests the Persian Gulf, but they are two pieces. Taking D out of INDIA gives INIA. Abyssinia is the old name of Ethiopia.
explanation.definitionFit: Abyssinia was the former name for the African country now called Ethiopia.

clue.text: Treat my daughter's in on for now

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Treat my daughter's in on for now', anagrams 'my daughter's in on' with 'Treat', but 'for now' cannot define Mothering Sunday; the definition looks garbled in the OCR.
annotationWithheld.clue: Treat my daughter's in on for now

clue.text: Henry I in time a source of artistic inspiration

indicators.note: in says that Henry and the I sit inside the letters for time and a

parts.note: Hal is the familiar short form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal
the letter I taken as written

explanation.surface: King Henry the First turns up at some point in history as a muse.
explanation.walkthrough: HAL plus I goes inside T and A. Thalia is one of the nine Muses, the one for comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Thalia is the Muse of comedy, and the Muses were said to give artists their inspiration.

clue.text: Influences from demon drink in the end disappearing

parts.note: an imp is a small demon

indicators.note: the end disappearing means one letter is lost from the end of the word for drink in

parts.note: to drink something in is to take it in, or ingest it

explanation.surface: Things that sway someone, starting with a devilish drink, eventually fade away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the end disappearing' takes T out of INGESTS. Note 'drink in' is one idea, to take in, not a drink plus 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: To impinge on something is to have an effect on it, so both verbs mean affecting.

clue.text: Teddy in a novel and a set of old articles

parts.note: Teddy is a pet name for Edward

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of the two words take a new order

explanation.surface: A teddy bear appears in a story along with some antiques.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' reads as a book, but it rearranges IN A to IAN. Edwardiana are things from the reign of Edward VII, 1901-10.
explanation.definitionFit: Collections of objects from Edward VII's era, early last century, are known by this name.

clue.text: Maybe Lancashire don's opposite, frustrated

parts.note: Lancashire is a crumbly English cheese, so it is an example of one
to don a hat is to put it on; to doff it is to take it off

explanation.surface: A Lancashire academic's opposite number is fed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'don' reads like a university lecturer, but it is the verb to put on; its opposite is DOFF.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheesed off is British slang for being annoyed, fed up or exasperated.

clue.text: Makes ready to cross a river with baths for transport?

indicators.note: to cross means the outer word goes across, around, the three small pieces

parts.note: to cash a cheque is to turn it into ready money

explanation.surface: Someone gets ready to cross a river and bathe on the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes ready' gives CASHES (turns into ready money), which goes around A, R and W.
explanation.definitionFit: Car washes clean vehicles, so they are, whimsically, baths for one's transport.

clue.text: Drawn out attempt to bask quietly?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Drawn out attempt to bask quietly?', has no indicator that could put P into SUN, and no other parse gives SPUN; something seems missing from the OCR.
annotationWithheld.clue: Drawn out attempt to bask quietly?

clue.text: Gossip as school marks slowly emerge

parts.note: M stands for marks, the old German currency
to ooze is to seep out slowly

explanation.surface: Chatter spreads as the exam results trickle out at a school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'marks' suggests exam grades; it is the old German currency, the Deutschmark, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: To schmooze is to chat in a sociable, ingratiating way, as gossiping is chatting.

clue.text: Hair in knee-length locks in place of curlers

indicators.note: the words lock in the answer, which runs across them without a break

explanation.surface: Long hair hanging to the knees is held in place with curlers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hair' and 'curlers' suggest hairdressing; the curlers are players of curling, a sport on ice.
explanation.definitionFit: Curling is played on a sheet of ice called a rink, so that is where curlers are found.

clue.text: Enigmatic girl cooing — a lad gets upset

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A boy is put out by a girl's soft cooing.
explanation.walkthrough: COOING A LAD is rearranged. La Gioconda is the Italian name for the Mona Lisa, famous for her mysterious smile.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo's portrait of a woman with a mysterious smile is known in Italy by this name.

clue.text: Polished steel very violently

indicators.note: violently suggests the letters are thrown about into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Steel is polished really hard.
explanation.walkthrough: STEEL and V are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Svelte means sleek and graceful, so smooth or refined in style.

clue.text: At your review deal regularly in Hindu remedies

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter, starting with the first

explanation.surface: A doctor is asked to rate the Hindu treatments on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: Ayurveda is the traditional Hindu system of medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: Ayurveda is the ancient Indian system of healing, with its herbal cures and practices.

clue.text: Official, corrupt, swapping a couple of elements

indicators.note: I is the symbol for iodine and U for uranium, so two elements trade places in the word

parts.note: something corrupt is morally impure

explanation.surface: A dishonest official changes a couple of things around.
explanation.walkthrough: In IMPURE the I and the U change places, both being symbols of chemical elements.
explanation.definitionFit: An umpire is the official who rules on play in cricket, tennis and other sports.

clue.text: Girl hosting publicity dodge

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so the girl's name holds the publicity word

parts.note: Eve is a girl's name
an ad, short for advertisement, is publicity

explanation.surface: A woman throws a publicity stunt to avoid something.
explanation.definitionFit: To dodge a question or blow is to evade it, avoiding it skilfully.

clue.text: Drip — early signs of water in many places

indicators.note: early signs of means the opening letter of each word that follows

explanation.surface: Drops of water show up in lots of spots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drip' reads as drops of water, but it means a feeble person.
explanation.definitionFit: A drip is British slang for a weak, dull or ineffectual person, like a weakling.

clue.text: Song a hit once for all I could gather

indicators.note: gathering the letters up loosely into a heap mixes them into a new order

parts.words: a hit once for all I

explanation.surface: A singer says a hit from long ago seems familiar, as far as they can tell.
explanation.walkthrough: A HIT ONCE FOR ALL I is rearranged to give the famous Eagles song of 1977.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotel California is a famous rock song by the Eagles, a hit in the late 1970s.

clue.text: Good chap at Christmas missing university term

parts.note: a saint is a good person, abbreviated ST

indicators.note: missing means a letter is left out of the saint and the Christmas word

parts.note: Yule is an old name for Christmas

explanation.surface: A nice man at Christmas time doesn't go to college this term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing' drops U from ST YULE. 'term' is a verb: to style someone something is to call them that.
explanation.definitionFit: To style a person is to call or name them, just as to term them is.

clue.text: Plant producing cookers?

parts.note: cookers suggests ovens from a factory, but here they are cooking fruit, such as Bramleys, growing on a plant

explanation.surface: A factory turns out kitchen ovens.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooking apples, called cookers in Britain, grow on this kind of fruit tree in an orchard.
